fields.impactNotes: Three groups, very different exposure. Claims investigators (14 people) see the largest change: fraud triage is now model-first, so their queue arrives pre-ranked and their day shifts from finding candidates to investigating them. FNOL call handlers (40+) see almost nothing, one extra field on a screen. Claims managers get a new dashboard and a new question at monthly review, which is a reporting change rather than a workflow one. The investigators are the group that decides whether this succeeds, and they were not in the room for the PoC.
fields.commsNotes: Sequenced by exposure, not by seniority. Investigators first and in person, before any all-hands, because hearing it second-hand from a company-wide email is how this goes wrong. Then managers, then a short written note to call handlers. Fortnightly during rollout, then folded into the existing monthly claims meeting rather than kept as a separate AI update, which signals it is normal work now.
fields.resistanceNotes: Two expected objections, both reasonable. First, that the model will be used to measure investigator productivity: addressed by a written commitment that model agreement is not an individual performance metric, agreed with the claims director before rollout. Second, that a missed fraud will be blamed on the person who overrode the model: addressed by making override an explicitly supported action with a one-line reason field, and by reviewing overrides in aggregate rather than by name.
fields.adoptionNotes: Behavioural, not survey-based. Primary measure is override rate with reasons, reviewed monthly: a high rate means the model or the thresholds are wrong, not that the team is non-compliant, and that framing is stated to the team. Secondary is time-to-first-action on ranked claims. A satisfaction pulse runs quarterly but is treated as a lagging indicator.
